extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, public affairs, and public opinion (including journalists and press/PR writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for communicating news and shaping public opinion: how messages are produced, transmitted, and received across audiences and media, and what makes them effective or ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble comprehensive messaging machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Creel had to assemble machinery which included a Division of News that issued ... more than six thousand releases ... enlist seventy-five thousand Four Minute Men ... Boy scouts delivered annotated copies ... Fortnightly periodicals were sent to six hundred thousand teachers ... Two hundred thousand lantern slides ... fourteen hundred and thirty-eight different designs ... The chambers of commerce, the churches, fraternal societies, schools, were used as channels of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build diverse, large-scale distribution systems (press releases, speakers, printed materials, slides, posters, civic and voluntary organizations). Use multiple media and networks to saturate the target population; coordinate across public and private organizations to amplify reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure access across social enclaves and classes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are whole sections, there are vast groups, ghettoes, enclaves and classes that hear only vaguely about much that is going on. They live in grooves, are shut in among their own affairs ... barred out of larger affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which social sets or geographic communities are isolated from mainstream channels and design tailored outreach (local intermediaries, translated materials, in-person events) to reach them rather than assuming one uniform channel reaches all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for infrastructure, monopoly and cost barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopolizing of cables ... of ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, market places means ... a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion. But monopoly is not the only barrier. Cost and available supply are even greater ones ... if the cost of travelling or trading is prohibitive ... the barriers exist even without monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize physical, economic, and institutional constraints on circulation (cabling, transport, censorship, price). Plan around or mitigate these constraints (alternative channels, subsidized distribution, local partners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and income determine individual access
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income has considerable effect on his access to the world beyond his neighborhood. With money he can overcome almost every tangible obstacle of communication, he can travel, buy books and periodicals ... The income of the individual, and the income of the community determine the amount of communication that is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by economic capacity and provide accessible formats and distribution for lower-income groups (free or low-cost formats, radio, local meetings) since paid channels may exclude them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and design for audience appetite and curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: There are portions of the sovereign people who spend most of their spare time and spare money on motoring ... bridge-whist and post-mortems, on moving-pictures and potboilers, talking always to the same people with minute variations ... They suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume equal interest in public affairs; craft messaging to engage attention, use hooks relevant to the audience's interests, and accept that some groups will need stronger provocation or simpler entry points to engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor social-set norms and the custodians of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: In the social set ... opinions encounter the canons of Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form, which make up the social set's picture of itself ... Within each social set there are augurs ... recognized as the custodians and the interpreters of its social pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and work with the opinion leaders and cultural gatekeepers of each social set; tailor tone, examples, and framing to the set's norms and values to gain acceptance and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target 'radiant points' and influential elites
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the sets are so placed that they become ... 'radiant points of conventionality.' Thus the social superior is likely to be imitated by the social inferior ... The powerful, socially superior, successful, rich, urban social set is fundamentally international ... It is at once a great circle of talk and a real social set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize influential social groups and elites whose behavior and tastes diffuse widely; securing their attention can cascade imitation and spread your message more effectively than trying to reach all audiences equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for limited time and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Over three quarters ... rate rather low the attention they give to printed news of the outer world ... Nearly seventy-one percent based their conscious preference on local news ... these figures ... show that the time each day is small when any of us is directly exposed to information from our unseen environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume small windows of attention (empirical estimates ~15 minutes/day for news readers). Put the essential facts and framing up front (lead with the key point), keep messages brief, and make it easy to grasp the main takeaway quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content to audience preferences and media space
rubrics_metrics.description: College students ... picked as the most interesting features news and opinion that dealt with public affairs ... Scott's group preferred local, political, financial, foreign, general, or editorials. Wilcox's analysis shows newspapers allocate substantial space to war, general, special features, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose angle and emphasis that align with the target outlet's and audience's preferences (local angle for local papers, financial angle for business readership). Understand typical editorial space allocation to increase pick-up likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple media and illustrative formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourteen hundred and thirty-eight different designs were turned out for posters, window cards, newspaper advertisements, cartoons, seals and buttons ... Two hundred thousand lantern slides were furnished for illustrated lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augment text with visual, auditory, and in-person materials (posters, slides, images, talks). Diverse formats help penetrate different social sets and compensate for limited textual attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate speed-and-coding constraints of wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: Telegraphy is expensive, and the facilities are often limited. Press service news is, therefore, usually coded. ... a dispatch ... may pass over the wires in the following form: 'Washn i. The Uni Stas rgds tq of Ger spg seized ...' ... The substance has been culled from a long speech in a foreign tongue, translated, coded, and then decoded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing copy for wire or terse distribution, compress information into the smallest clear units, avoid dependence on nuance-heavy phrasing that will be lost in coding, and provide clear synopses that survive abbreviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack meaning into few words but expect loss of nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: A few words must often stand for a whole succession of acts, thoughts, feelings and consequences ... It is doubtful whether a supreme master of style could pack all the elements of truth ... into a hundred word account ... Words are imperfect vehicles of meanings. ... There is no certainty whatever that the same word will call out exactly the same idea in the reader's mind as it did in the reporter's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity over elegance; choose words that minimize ambiguity, supply concise context cues, and, where possible, offer links or references for fuller detail because short accounts will omit complexities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sources and context to help judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement charging ... was issued here to-day by the Korean Commission, based, the Commission said, on authentic reports received by it from Manchuria. ... eyewitnesses, their accuracy unknown, report to the makers of 'authentic reports'; they in turn transmit these to a commission five thousand miles away. The meaning has to be telescoped in such a way as to permit the reader to judge how much weight to give to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When space allows, indicate provenance and reliability of information (eyewitness, commission report, corroboration) so recipients can assess credibility; be transparent about limits and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate language for cultural/linguistic differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, like currency, are tokens of value. ... Expressions such as 'a distinguished scholar,' 'a clever writer,' must be translated into French as 'a great savant,' 'an exquisite master.' ... Nations that understate keep their word-currency sound. Nations that overstate suffer from inflation in their language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of cross-cultural tone and translation: idioms and degrees (e.g., 'distinguished') do not map directly across languages. Avoid hyperbole that may be amplified or misread; when translating provide annotations or calibrated equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for lucidity: discriminate and avoid crude analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind ... The quality ... is the power to discriminate among crude perceptions and vague analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sweeping analogies or lumping disparate phenomena together; make key distinctions explicit (who, what, when, where, why) so readers can form more precise mental models rather than relying on vague stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt vocabulary/readability to audience capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Millions of those who are watching him can read hardly at all. Millions more can read the words but cannot understand them. Of those who can both read and understand, a good three-quarters ... have some part of half an hour a day to spare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language and accessible sentence structures for broad audiences; where targeted to specialists, use technical language, but for the general public supply simple summaries or lead paragraphs that convey the essential meaning.
